newsitem.title: USA: Pataki takes Earth Day aim on sooty buses, trucks.
newsitem.headline: Pataki takes Earth Day aim on sooty buses, trucks.

text.p: New York Gov. George Pataki made an Earth Day declaration of war Tuesday on sooty air, introducing legislation that would submit diesel-burning buses and heavy trucks to annual emissions tests.

The aim of the bill is to cleanse the air of one of the biggest banes of big-city life: the dark, noxious -- and suspected carcinogenic -- particulate matter that buses and heavy trucks often belch directly into the faces of pedestrians.

"This legislation will help clean up the black soot we've all seen pouring out of buses and trucks and provide cleaner, healthier air for New Yorkers, particularly residents of New York City," Pataki said.

Pataki, a Republican governor often given good marks by environmentalists, said the legislation would require the state Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) to implement the pollution-testing program by Dec. 31, 1998.
Cheered on by numerous environmental groups, he announced the legislation Tuesday at Manhattan Bridge Plaza, an area of New York City with the highest levels for particulate matter.

The federal Environmental Protection Agency has described particulates as a possible human carcinogen and heavy duty vehicles are the primary source, with levels in New York City currently exceeding federal standards.

Under the proposed rules, the emission control systems of diesel-powered trucks and buses weighing more than 8,500 pounds would be tested at service garages and repaired, if necessary. The state inspection fee is expected to range from $20 to $40.
And out-of-state vehicles venturing through the Empire State could be pulled over for roadside inspections to make sure they pass environmental muster.
"Their vehicles would be given an opacity test -- to see how clearly you can see through a column of air," said Sam Thernstrom, a spokesman for the state DEC.
Offenders could be slapped with a $700 fine for a first violation and $1,300 for the second and subsequent violations, although the penalties would be reduced if repairs were made within 30 days.
With the introduction in recent years of cleaner burning low-sulfur diesel fuel, Thernstrom said most vehicles should have little problem complying with the new standards.
"But some vehicles would probably need engine repairs," he added, "most likely to the fuel injection pump."
Ken Scallon, program director of the American Lung Assocication of New York State, told Reuters he was optimistic the plan could give medical relief to many of the state's 920,000 asthmatics.

Pataki last year directed state agencies to implement a stringent emission testing system for passenger automobiles in New York City and adjacent counties. The new test, made during annual auto inspections, begins in November.
